summary: Adds three methods to CoAP: FETCH, PATCH and iPATCH. The original CoAP methods only work on a whole resource, which is wasteful for large or complex data. These new ones let a client read or update just part of a resource.

eli5.summary: Instead of copying a whole book to change one word, you just say which word to change. These new commands let tiny devices do that.

questions: how to update part of a coap resource
what is the difference between patch and ipatch
subtitle: Three new CoAP methods that let small devices read or change just part of a resource.

tldr.problem: CoAP's GET and PUT only deal with a whole resource, and GET cannot carry a request body. Apps that need to query part of a resource or change part of it end up misusing POST.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8132 adds FETCH (a GET-like request that carries a body), plus PATCH and iPATCH, which apply a described set of changes to a resource. iPATCH is the idempotent variant.
tldr.outcome: Clients can fetch or update only the pieces they care about, saving traffic on constrained links. The methods get codes 0.05, 0.06 and 0.07 in the CoAP method registry.

today: RFC 8132 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is still the definition of the CoAP FETCH, PATCH and iPATCH methods.

sections.title: Why CoAP Needed New Methods
sections.content:
As in HTTP, the GET method in RFC 7252 only lets a client name a URI and a few options. It cannot send a request payload that says in detail what is wanted. Likewise PUT can only replace a complete resource. Applications that want a cacheable, safe query, or a partial update, therefore tend to fall back on POST.

This document adds FETCH, which is like a GET with a request body, and the twin methods PATCH and iPATCH, which modify parts of a resource. The RFC notes that PATCH was not adopted early in CoAP's design, but partial updates became necessary for applications such as CoAP management, and sending only the change spares the constrained communication medium.
sections.eli5: Before, a tiny device could only ask for the whole toy box or swap the whole toy box. Now it can ask for one toy, or change one toy.

sections.title: The FETCH Method
sections.content:
FETCH asks the server to produce a representation described by the request parameters, meaning the options plus the payload, based on the resource at the request URI. The result is not assumed to be a complete representation of the resource, so a cache cannot reuse it to answer a GET. The body may be built with block-wise transfer.

FETCH is both safe and idempotent: it is not meant to change the target resource. Responses can be cached depending on the response code, with the request body being part of the cache key; a 2.05 (Content) response is the typical answer. A request MUST include a Content-Format option to say what media type and content coding the body has. A client cannot build a FETCH from a link alone, since it also needs a way to produce the payload.

The Observe option can be used with FETCH as with GET, and Block1 is used as it would be with POST. If the request carries If-Match or If-None-Match, it becomes a conditional FETCH, and the conditions are checked against the target resource itself, not the FETCH results.

The RFC's example uses a made-up media type, application/example-map-keys+json, to pick just the key foo out of a JSON object at coap://www.example.com/object; the server answers 2.05 Content with only that member.
sections.eli5: FETCH is like handing the librarian a note saying exactly which pages you want, instead of asking for the whole book.

sections.title: PATCH and iPATCH
sections.content:
PATCH and iPATCH ask the server to apply a set of changes, described in the request payload in some media type, to the target resource. If the URI does not point to an existing resource, the server MAY create one, depending on the patch document type and permissions; that gives a 2.01 (Created) response. If-Match and If-None-Match can restrict a request.

PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent. iPATCH is not safe but is idempotent, like CoAP PUT. Marking a request as idempotent is the only difference between the two, and it may let a server keep less state, so some constrained servers may implement only iPATCH. Servers that do not rely on idempotence are RECOMMENDED to support both.

Both are atomic: the server MUST apply the whole set of changes or none, and never show a partly modified representation to a concurrent GET. This applies to a single server only; for a multicast request, an atomic commit across servers is out of scope. A 2.01 response invalidates cache entries for the resource named by the Location options, and a 2.04 (Changed) response invalidates the target's cache entry.
sections.eli5: PATCH is like handing over a sticky note saying fix this one word. It either gets fixed fully or not at all, never half done.

sections.title: PATCH Examples
sections.content:
The examples edit a JSON document with x-coord 256, y-coord 45 and foo set to ["bar","baz"]. An iPATCH using application/json-patch+json (Content-Format 51) replaces x-coord with 45 and gets 2.04 Changed. The same change with application/merge-patch+json (Content-Format 52) is just { "x-coord":45}.

A non-idempotent change shows the difference between the methods. Adding "bar" at foo/1 via iPATCH gets 4.00 Bad Request with the diagnostic "Patch format not idempotent" and leaves the document unchanged. The same request sent as PATCH succeeds with 2.04 Changed, and foo becomes ["bar","bar","baz"].
sections.eli5: If you say set the score to 45, saying it twice changes nothing. If you say add one more apple, saying it twice gives two apples, so only the plain PATCH is allowed to do that.

sections.title: Response Codes and Errors
sections.content:
Both FETCH and PATCH reuse the response codes and option numbers from RFC 7252. FETCH adds 4.13 (Request Entity Too Large), 4.15 (Unsupported Content-Format) and 4.22 (Unprocessable Entity). PATCH and iPATCH add 4.09 (Conflict) and 4.22.

Typical failures are a malformed payload (4.00), an unsupported payload (4.15), a valid payload the server cannot process (4.22), a payload too large (4.13), and for PATCH a missing resource (4.04) or a failed precondition (4.12). If a change would leave the resource in an inconsistent state the server cannot resolve, it can return 4.09 and SHOULD include enough information to show the source of the conflict. When concurrent requests to modify the same resource cannot be queued, or waiting takes too long, the server can return 5.03 (Service Unavailable).
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the server answers with a number that says what: your note was unreadable, too big, or two people tried to change the same thing at once.

sections.title: The New Set of Methods
sections.content:
The RFC argues that adding three methods to CoAP's existing four fits the REST paradigm and was anticipated on the HTTP side. Having both PATCH and iPATCH keeps interoperability with HTTP's PATCH while allowing a client to signal idempotence when possible, which saves significant effort on the server.

The new methods line up with the old ones in safety and idempotence: FETCH (0.05) is safe and idempotent like GET (0.01), PATCH (0.06) is neither like POST (0.02), and iPATCH (0.07) is idempotent but not safe, like PUT (0.03).
sections.eli5: The three new commands behave like cousins of the old ones: FETCH like GET, PATCH like POST, and iPATCH like PUT.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
FETCH is closest to GET, but its payload may reveal more detail about which parts of a resource the requester cares about than a plain GET for the whole resource would. Confidentiality protection by DTLS or other means may therefore be needed for FETCH where it would not be for GET.

PATCH and iPATCH are nearly identical to PUT in security terms, and the considerations of RFC 5789 also apply. Requests likely need authorization and protection against corruption or accidental overwrites. The new methods are secured following the existing CoAP recommendations.
sections.eli5: Asking for one specific page tells people what you are interested in, so you may want to whisper the request.
